name: Weights & Biases, Inc.
subcategory: ML experiment tracking / MLOps and LLMOps platform
origin_detail: Co-founded in 2017 in San Francisco by Lukas Biewald, Chris Van Pelt and Shawn Lewis; Biewald had earlier co-founded CrowdFlower/Figure Eight (2007), which Appen bought in 2019 for up to $300M
flagship_projects: W&B Models (experiment tracking, sweeps, artifacts, registry)
openness_notes: Initial 1, current 1. Only the client side is open: the wandb SDK repo has been public since 2017-03-24 and carries an MIT LICENSE file (added 2021-04-22), and the Weave LLM toolkit is Apache-2.0 (repo created 2023-06-07). The product people pay for, the tracking server and UI, is proprietary: it is sold as multi-tenant SaaS, dedicated cloud, or a self-managed W&B Server distributed as the wandb/local Docker image, where production features (external MySQL, cloud storage, SSO) need a licence from W&B. That is 'only peripheral SDKs/clients open' (level 1). No relicensing in either direction was found.

license_history.note: Repo created 2017-03-24; LICENSE file (MIT) only added 2021-04-22, so the earlier formal licence is not confirmed from fetched pages

license_history.license: W&B Server: proprietary Docker image (wandb/local); deployment repo MIT
license_history.note: wandb/server repo (created 2020-10-08) holds deployment docs; a free licence from the Deployer works for testing, a licence from W&B unlocks production features
LICENSE file created 2021-04-22 ('Create LICENSE (#2099)'), unchanged since
New LLM application toolkit, repo created 2023-06-07

exit_events.note: Announced early March 2025 (reported 5 Mar 2025), weeks before CoreWeave's 28 Mar 2025 Nasdaq IPO; CoreWeave headline price ~$1.7B; Wikipedia gives closing on 5 May 2025. CoreWeave pledged continued interoperability with any infrastructure provider and model.

risk_events: 2025: acquired by GPU cloud CoreWeave (~$1.7B), raising vendor-neutrality questions for a tool used across all clouds; CoreWeave stated a commitment to interoperability
2025-2026: product folded into CoreWeave (docs moved to docs.coreweave.com, login via id.coreweave.com, blog at forge.coreweave.com; multi-tenant SaaS documented as 'Forge')
robustness: The open MIT client is embedded in more than 20,000 open-source repositories (2023), but the server, data store and UI are proprietary and now owned by CoreWeave, so users depend on one vendor's roadmap. Exports and the open SDK lower lock-in somewhat; there is no foundation or community governance.
physical_science_relevance: Widely used to track ML experiments in research; TechCrunch (2023) reported it cited in hundreds of academic papers, and it is common in ML-for-science training runs (e.g., model training for materials and biology).
openness_effect_assessment: A free, MIT-licensed client that plugged into every training script gave W&B a developer-led funnel (about 700,000 users, more than 1,000 of them paying, by Aug 2023, with OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere and Hugging Face as users) while the monetized server stayed closed. Openness was a distribution tactic, not the product: the company never opened the server and still reached a $1.25B valuation (2023) and a ~$1.7B sale (2025).
key_takeaway: Weights & Biases shows the AI-era 'open client, closed service' model: an MIT SDK spread through the ML community, but the value captured was in the proprietary hosted platform, which a GPU cloud (CoreWeave) bought for ~$1.7B in 2025 to move up the stack from compute to developer tools. It is an exit for a mostly closed product, not evidence that an open-source licence itself was the business.
